title: Zeus in the comedy and the one corner
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τοιαῦτά τινα λέγει ὁ Κέλσος· ἔτι μὴν εἴπερ ἐβούλετο ὁ θεὸς ὥσπερ ὁ παρὰ τῷ κωμῳδῷ Ζεὺς ἐκ τοῦ μακροῦ ὕπνου διϋπνίσας ῥύσασθαι τὸ (τῶν) ἀνθρώπων γένος ἐκ κακῶν, τί δή ποτε εἰς μίαν γωνίαν ἔπεμψε τοῦτο, ὅ φατε, πνεῦμα; δέον πολλὰ ὁμοίως διαφυσῆσαι σώματα καὶ κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀποστεῖλαι τὴν οἰκουμένην. ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν κωμῳδὸς ἐν τῷ θεάτρῳ γελωτοποιῶν συνέγραψεν ὅτι Ζεὺς ἐξυπνισθεὶς Ἀθηναίοις καὶ Λακεδαιμονίοις τὸν Ἑρμῆν ἔπεμψε· σὺ δὲ οὐκ οἴει καταγελαστότερον πεποιηκέναι Ἰουδαίοις πεμπόμενον τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν υἱόν; ὅρα δὴ καὶ ἐν τούτοις τὸ ἄσεμνον τοῦ Κέλσου, ἀφιλοσόφως κωμῳδίας ποιητὴν γελωτοποιὸν παραλαβόντος καὶ τῷ παρ᾿ αὐτῷ διϋπνισθέντι πέμποντι Ἑρμῆν παραβάλλοντος τὸν τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν. εἴπομεν δὴ ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτων ὅτι οὐχ ὥσπερ ἀπὸ μακροῦ ὕπνου διαναστὰς ὁ θεὸς ἔπεμψε τὸν Ἰησοῦν τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώ πων, τὴν μὲν κατὰ τὴν ἐνσωμάτωσιν οἰκονομίαν νῦν δι᾿ εὐλόγους αἰτίας ἐπικληρώσαντα ἀεὶ δὲ τὸ γένος τῶν ἀνθρώπων εὐεργετήσαντα. οὐδὲν γὰρ τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις καλῶν γεγένηται, μὴ τοῦ θείου λόγου ἐπιδημήσαντος ταῖς ψυχαῖς τῶν κἂν ὀλίγον καιρὸν δεδυνημένων δέξασθαι τὰς τοιάσδε τοῦ θείου λόγου ἐνεργείας. ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡ δοκοῦσα εἰς μίαν γωνίαν ἐπιδημία τοῦ Ἰησοῦ εὐλόγως γεγένηται, ἐπείπερ ἐχρῆν τοῖς ἕνα θεὸν μεμαθηκόσι καὶ τοὺς προφήτας αὐτοῦ ἀναγινώσκουσι καὶ κηρυσσόμενον Χριστὸν μανθάνουσιν ἐπιδημῆσαι τὸν προφητευόμενον καὶ ἐπιδημῆσαι ἐν καιρῷ, ὅτ᾿ ἔμελλεν ἐκχεῖσθαι ἀπὸ μιᾶς γωνίας ὁ λόγος ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν οἰκουμένην.
pass_a_gloss: Next Celsus says (λέγει) such things: 'Further, if God wished (ἐβούλετο), like the Zeus in the comic poet (κωμῳδός), having woken (διϋπνίσας) from long sleep (ὕπνος), to rescue (ῥύσασθαι) the race of humans from evils, why ever did he send into one corner (γωνία) this, which you call, spirit (πνεῦμα)? It was necessary (δέον) to blow/breathe (διαφυσῆσαι) many bodies alike and send them out over the whole inhabited world (οἰκουμένη). But the comic poet, making laughter (γελωτοποιῶν) in the theatre, wrote that Zeus, woken, sent Hermes to Athenians and Lacedaemonians; and do you not think you have made it more laughable (καταγελαστότερον), the Son of God being sent to Jews?' See in these things too the unseemliness (τὸ ἄσεμνον) of Celsus, unphilosophically (ἀφιλοσόφως) taking up a laughter-making comic poet and comparing (παραβάλλοντος) with the one in him who woke and sent Hermes the Maker (δημιουργός) of the all, our God. We said in what precedes that not as rising from long sleep did God send Jesus to the race of humans, having now for reasonable causes (εὐλόγους αἰτίας) allotted/brought to pass (ἐπικληρώσαντα) the economy (οἰκονομία) concerning embodiment (ἐνσωμάτωσις), but having always benefited (εὐεργετήσαντα) the race of humans. For nothing of the good things among humans has come to be without the divine Word (θεῖος λόγος) sojourning (ἐπιδημήσαντος) in the souls of those able even for a little time to receive such workings (ἐνεργείας) of the divine Word. But also the seeming coming into one corner of Jesus has happened reasonably, since it was needful that to those who had learned one God, reading his prophets and learning a proclaimed (κηρυσσόμενον) Christ, the prophesied one should come, and come at a time when the Word was about to be poured out (ἐκχεῖσθαι) from one corner over the whole inhabited world.
pass_b_english: Next Celsus says something like this: “Moreover, if God, like Zeus in the comic poet, woke from his long sleep and wished to rescue the human race from evils, why did he send this spirit, as you call it, into one corner? He ought to have breathed it alike into many bodies and sent them out over the whole world. But the comic poet was raising a laugh in the theatre when he wrote that Zeus woke up and sent Hermes to the Athenians and the Spartans; do you not think you have made a more laughable thing of it, with the Son of God sent to the Jews?”

See here too how unseemly Celsus is. Quite unlike a philosopher, he takes up a comic poet whose business is laughter, and he compares our God, the Maker of the universe, with that poet’s Zeus, who wakes up and sends Hermes. We said earlier that God did not send Jesus to the human race as though he had risen from a long sleep. For good reasons he has now carried out the dispensation of the incarnation, but he has always done good to the human race. For nothing good among men has come about without the divine Word coming to dwell in the souls of those who were able, even for a short time, to receive such workings of the divine Word. Moreover, the coming of Jesus, which seems to have been into one corner, took place for good reason. The one foretold had to come to those who had come to know the one God, who read his prophets and were learning of the Christ proclaimed to them; and he had to come at the time when the Word was about to be poured out from one corner over the whole world.

choices.choice: The whole first paragraph is Celsus’s quotation, including the second sentence about the comic poet and the ‘you’ addressed to Christians; Origen’s reply begins at ‘See here too’. The comedy is not named by Celsus or Origen and is uncertain (possibly a lost play), so no source citation is given. ‘Lacedaemonians’ rendered ‘Spartans’. ‘Spirit’ in Celsus’s mouth is lowercase: he means the divine spirit he spoke of in Jesus’s body (6.77), not a confession of the Holy Spirit. διαφυσῆσαι (blow through, breathe into) rendered ‘breathed it alike into’. ἐπικληρώσαντα (‘allotted, assigned’) rendered ‘carried out’; ἐνσωμάτωσις (‘embodiment’) rendered ‘incarnation’. ἐχρῆν (‘it had to be’) rendered ‘had to come’, not the weaker ‘it was fitting’. κηρυσσόμενον Χριστόν (‘a Christ being proclaimed’) rendered ‘the Christ proclaimed to them’, without naming who proclaims. ὁ λόγος in the last clause is capitalised ‘Word’: the next chapter goes on with the one Word rising as the sun of righteousness; it may also mean the Christian message. ‘One corner’ is Celsus’s phrase; a possible contrast with Acts 26:26 (‘this was not done in a corner’) is not marked by Origen and is not cited. ‘Earlier’ refers back to Origen’s previous answers to the charge that God sent Christ so late (the exact passage is not named here).
ἔτι μήν: 'Again' -> 'Moreover'; 'a long sleep' -> 'his long sleep' (article)
kept the ἀλλά...δέ contrast in Celsus's comic-poet sentence ('But the comic poet was raising a laugh... do you not think')
ἀφιλοσόφως: 'With no philosophy in it' -> 'Quite unlike a philosopher'; γελωτοποιόν -> 'whose business is laughter'
ἐχρῆν: 'It was fitting' -> 'had to come' (necessity, not fitness)
κηρυσσόμενον Χριστόν: 'the Christ they proclaimed' -> 'the Christ proclaimed to them' (removed added agency); ἕνα θεὸν μεμαθηκόσι -> 'had come to know the one God'
notes updated for the changes and for capitalised Word
